clauses: The boys have come out on the porch to blow bubbles.
"Ha, ha!" laughs Robert, as a bubble comes down softly on the old cat's back, and does not burst.
Willie tries to make his bubble do the same, and it comes down on the cat's face, and makes her sneeze.
"She would rather wash her face without soap," says Harry. "Now let us see who can make the biggest bubble."
"Mine is the biggest," says Robert. "See how high it floats in the air! It has burst."
"I can see the house and the trees and the sky in mine," says Willie; "and such beautiful colors."
"I know how many colors there are," says Harry. "Just as many as there are in the rainbow."
note: 3 same-gender boys (Robert, Willie, Harry) co-present blowing bubbles, each taking speaking turns with postposed 'says X' quotative attribution and no pronoun link back to a prior mention; recency-chain-everything baseline cannot distinguish speaker identity across turns since all 3 are equally recent/salient candidates.

clauses: So Sam walked on, very sad.
Soon after, a fine carriage came up, and in it were Harry and his mother.
The blind man stood, and held out his hat.
"Let us give the poor man something," said Harry to his mother.
His mother gave him some cents, and Harry took them, but did not put them into the man's hat.
He threw them into the hedge as far as he could, and the poor man could not find them, for he was blind.
Sam had turned back to look at the fine carriage, and he saw Harry throw the cents into the hedge.
So Sam came back at once, and looked for the money until he found it all for the blind man.
note: Two named boys (Sam, Harry) plus a blind man co-present; 'He' in clause 5 (threw cents into hedge) is same-gender-ambiguous with Sam and Harry both available antecedents from surrounding clauses, resolving to Harry; clause 6 'he saw Harry' requires distinguishing Sam (resumed protagonist, absent for 5 clauses) from Harry (most recent named boy) -- a genuine long-distance same-gender reactivation trap, not simple recency.

clauses: "Sit still, children, do not move about in the boat," said Mr. Rose to the young folks he was taking for a trip on the water.
There were in the boat Mr. Rose, the boatman, and several little boys and girls.
"Keep still, please, young gentlemen," said the boatman, when Edgar Rose and Thomas Read began to move from one side to the other.
They kept quiet for a short time only, and Edgar soon wanted a stick which Thomas held in his hand.
He lost his balance in trying to get the stick, and fell into the water.
Mr. Rose started up, and stretched out his arms to save him, but in so doing, they upset the boat.
note: Edgar and Thomas are both boys named in the same clause (clause 2); 'He' in clause 4 (lost his balance and fell) is a same-gender antecedent choice between them, resolving to Edgar (the agent of 'wanted a stick') not Thomas (who merely held it) -- recency alone favors Thomas (mentioned last in clause 3) which would be WRONG.

clauses: One winter night, Mrs. Lord and her two little girls sat by a bright fire in their pleasant home.
At last, Katie finished her work, and, looking up, said, "Mother, I think the fire is brighter than usual."
"And I was about to say," cried Mary, "that this is a better light than we had last night."
"My dears," said their mother, "it must be that you feel happier than usual to-night."
"But, mother," said Mary, "I do not see why we are happier now than we were then."
"I know why!" said Katie. "It is because we have all been doing something useful to-night."
"You are right, my dear," said their mother, "I am glad you have both learned that."
note: Two named girls (Katie, Mary) plus their mother, all three female (same 'she'-class); rapid alternating quotative turns ('said Katie'/'cried Mary'/'said their mother') require tracking WHICH of 3 same-gender entities is speaking each turn, not pronoun gender.

clauses: Willie had strolled with Bounce down to the river, which was not more than two blocks from his father's store.
Bounce lay on the grass, watching the flies that buzzed around his nose.
Willie jumped upon one of the logs floating near the shore, to see if he could throw a stone across the river.
He drew back, and sent the stone with all his might; just as it left his hand, the log turned, and he fell into the water.
Poor little Bounce gave a great yelp of distress, and ran up and down the bank, barking, looking first at Willie and then around.
Then Bounce started, as fast as he could run, up the street to the store, and scratched against the door until Mr. Brown opened it.
He caught hold of Mr. Brown's clothes, then ran to the door, then back again, catching at him, barking, and jumping.
Brown thought of Willie, and as he came to the river, he saw Willie's hat floating on the water, and sprang in and caught him just in time.
note: Willie (boy), Bounce (male dog), and Mr. Brown (father) are ALL referred to with 'he/him' -- a cross-species same-pronoun-class trap. Clause 6 'He caught hold of Mr. Brown's clothes' requires resolving 'He'=Bounce (not Willie, absent from the scene at the river; not Brown, named in the same clause as patient) purely from event structure, testing whether coref is animacy-aware or purely recency/gender based.

clauses: James White has two dogs; one is a Newfoundland dog, and the other is a Scotch terrier.
Sport is a good watchdog, and every night he guards the house while James and his father are asleep.
In the daytime, James often uses Sport for his horse, and hitches Sport to a little wagon.
The name of James's Scotch terrier is Dodger; he is called Dodger because he jumps about so friskily.
Dodger has very bright eyes, and he does many funny things.
The other day he took baby's red stocking, and had great fun with it, but he spoiled it in his play, and James had to scold him.
note: James (boy) and his two dogs Sport and Dodger are ALL referenced with 'he' -- a three-way same-gender-class trap across species. Clause 5 stacks 'he took...he spoiled...James had to scold him' in one sentence: the first two 'he' = Dodger (agent), 'him' = Dodger (patient of scold), James is the only entity named by proper noun -- requires distinguishing 3 same-pronoun referents within a single clause.

clauses: "Mamma," said George West, as he came from school, "I can't help thinking about that poor little girl I told you of the other day."
"Suppose you should carry her a handful of pretty flowers some time," said his mother.
"Did you use to live in the country?" asked George. "Oh, yes," answered Jennie, "we used to live in a beautiful cottage."
"Well, what made you move here?" "Papa died, and mamma was sick so long that the money was all gone," said Jennie.
"Mamma," said George, that evening, "papa must give them some money, so they can go back to their home."
"No," said his mother, "he can not do that, but perhaps he can help us contrive some way to assist them."
note: The word 'mamma' refers to TWO DIFFERENT people depending on which child is speaking: George's mother (clauses 0,1,4,5) versus Jennie's mother (clause 3, mentioned but never co-present). This is harder than pronoun coref -- the SAME common noun is not coreferent across speakers. Director should verify this is intended difficulty (a genuine same-noun-different-referent trap) rather than corpus artifact before use.

clauses: Fred was wakened by the alarm and the red light streaming into his room, and hurried to the fire.
"It is Mr. Barton's house, mother, do let me go," he said in eager, excited tones.
Fred found Tom outside, in safety. "Where is Katy?" he asked.
Tom, trembling with terror, said, "Katy is in the house!"
"In what room?" asked Fred. "In that one," Tom answered, pointing to a window in the upper story.
There was but one way to reach Katy, and Fred knew it, but he trusted in an arm stronger than his own.
note: Fred and Tom are both boys in a fast multi-turn rescue dialogue; 'he asked' (clause 2) and the implicit speaker alternation in clauses 3-4 require tracking conversational turn-taking between two same-gender entities, not pronoun gender; Katy is the absent third entity being discussed (referential target, never co-present as a speaker) -- a useful discussed-vs-present contrast.

clauses: "Come, come," said Master Sharp, "I am within one inch of the mark."
John drew his bow, and shot, and the arrow struck within a quarter of an inch of Master Sharp's.
"Shoot away," said Sharp, "but you must understand the rules; nobody is to borrow or lend."
John seized his second arrow; "If I have any luck," said he; but just then the string broke, and the arrow fell from his hands.
It was now Ben's turn to make his trial; his first arrow missed the mark, and the second was exactly as near as John's first.
Master Sharp clapped his hands and danced for joy, but his dancing suddenly ceased, when careful Ben drew an excellent piece of cord from his pocket.
"The everlasting whipcord, I declare!" cried John. "Yes," said Ben, "I put it in my pocket today because I thought I might want it."
note: Three male entities (Sharp, John, Ben) in an archery contest with dense 'his' possessives; clause 5 'his dancing suddenly ceased, when careful Ben drew...' requires distinguishing Sharp's 'his' (subject of the main clause) from Ben (introduced immediately after in the same sentence) -- a same-gender antecedent-choice trap where the two candidates are adjacent.

clauses: "Beg, Frisk, beg," said little Harry, as he sat on an inverted basket, eating a porringer of bread and milk.
His little sister Annie, who had already dispatched her breakfast, sat on the ground opposite to him, twisting her flowers into garlands.
"Beg, Frisk, beg!" repeated Harry, holding a bit of bread just out of the dog's reach, and the obedient Frisk squatted himself on his hind legs, waiting for Harry to give him the morsel.
Frisk loved him dearly, much better than he did anyone else, because he recollected that Harry was his earliest and firmest friend.
Harry took a fancy to him, and Harry's grandmother, who drove him off with a broom, at length let the little dog remain.
He could fetch or carry either by land or water, and would pick up a ball of cotton if little Annie should happen to drop it, or take Harry's dinner to school for him.
note: Harry (boy), Frisk (male dog), and Annie (sister) co-present; clause 3 'he did anyone else...he recollected' is a cross-species same-gender-class trap ambiguous between Frisk (agent of 'loved') and Harry (topic of 'recollected'); Annie is the sole female contrast entity in the scene.

clauses: "I will have revenge on him, that I will," said Philip to himself, with a countenance quite red with anger.
"Who is that," said Stephen, "on whom you intend to be revenged?"
"It was farmer Robinson's son who reduced it to this worthless state," replied Philip.
Stephen coolly asked him what had induced young Robinson to break it.
"He came up close to me, and began to call me names," replied Philip, "but I will make him repent of it."
"To be sure," said Stephen, "he is a very wicked boy, and nobody likes him or will have anything to do with him."
"All this is true," replied Philip, "but he has broken my cane, and I will be revenged."
note: Philip, Stephen, and the absent third boy (Robinson's son) are all male; clauses 4-6 stack multiple 'he/him' per sentence referring to different combinations of the three (e.g. clause 4 'He came up...I will make him repent' = Robinson's son as agent then patient within one line while Philip is the speaker) -- one of the densest same-gender pronoun-chain passages found in the corpus.

clauses: Lucy very kindly took up the kite and threw it into the air, but her brother neglecting to run off, the kite fell down again.
Lucy once more took up the kite, but John was in too great a hurry; he ran off so suddenly that he twitched the kite out of her hand.
"Well, who is to blame now?" asked Lucy. "Try again," said I.
"There, there!" exclaimed John, "that comes of your throwing it all to one side." "As if I could make the wind blow straight," said Lucy.
"O John, you should not have stopped," said I. "However, try again."
"You may thank aunt for it, brother," said Lucy, "for you would have given it up long ago, if she had not persuaded you."
note: Lucy (girl), John (boy), and the aunt-narrator ('I' in clauses 2/4, referred to in THIRD PERSON as 'aunt' by Lucy in clause 5) are co-present; clause 5 requires recognizing that 'aunt' = the same referent as the first-person 'I' from earlier clauses -- a person-deixis coref shift (1st-person narrator to 3rd-person same-referent) layered on top of standard entity tracking. Lucy and the aunt share gender.

clauses: Michael and Agnes were childless, and Michael said to a man near him, "She has sunk into some mossy or miry place."
A man came running toward the place where Michael and others were standing beside Agnes, who lay exhausted on the sward.
Michael saw that he carried Lucy's bonnet, clothes, and plaid.
Isabel took the clothes, and, narrowly inspecting them, said, "No, Lucy is yet among the living."
Agnes had been able to walk home, and Michael and Isabel sat by her bedside.
"I hear footsteps coming up the brae," said Agnes, and in a few moments the voice of Jacob Mayne was heard at the door.
Michael stood up between Jacob and his wife, and looked into his heart.
note: Four entities in two same-gender pairs: Agnes/Isabel (both female) and Michael/Jacob (both male) -- a rare 2x2 gender-paired configuration. Clause 6 'Michael stood up between Jacob and his wife' has 'his' ambiguous between Michael and Jacob (both male, both present); resolving requires knowing whose wife is present (Michael's), not just recency.

clauses: "Sing some more, dear," said Madam, in her gentle way, when Polly had done.
"That's a jolly tune! Sing it again, please," cried Tom's voice, and there was Tom's red head bobbing up over the chair.
"I can't sing any more; I'm tired," Polly said, and walked away to Madam, and the red head vanished.
"You mus'n't mind my staring, dear," said Madam, "I haven't seen a little girl for so long." Polly asked, "Aren't Fan and Maud little girls, too?"
"Oh, dear, no!" said Madam. "Fan has been a young lady this two years, and Maud is a spoiled baby."
"That's the way I was brought up, and that's why Fan calls me old-fashioned," said Madam. "Tell more about your papa," said Polly.
note: Five entities: Madam, Polly, and Tom are directly co-present/speaking; Fan and Maud are named and discussed within the same turn as Polly ('Aren't Fan and Maud little girls, too?'). Four female referents (Madam, Polly, Fan, Maud) total, one of the densest same-gender scenes mined; Tom is the lone male contrast, introduced only by his voice/head (partial presence).

clauses: "Come," said Squeers, "let's go to the schoolroom, and lend me a hand with my school coat."
Nicholas assisted his master to put on an old jacket, and Squeers, arming himself with his cane, led the way across the yard.
"This is our shop, Nickleby," said the schoolmaster, as they stepped in together.
"Now," said Squeers, giving the desk a great rap with his cane, "is that physicking over?"
"Just over," said Mrs. Squeers, choking the last boy in her hurry, and tapping the crown of his head with the wooden spoon.
Smike shuffled out with the basin, and Mrs. Squeers hurried out after him into the washhouse.
"This is the first class in English spelling and philosophy, Nickleby," said Squeers, beckoning Nicholas to stand beside him.
note: Squeers (schoolmaster), Nicholas/'Nickleby' (usher), Mrs. Squeers, and Smike (pupil) co-present; clause 1 'Nicholas assisted his master' -- 'his' resolves to Nicholas's employer (Squeers) not Nicholas himself, a role-dependent possessive-pronoun trap distinct from simple agent/patient coref; Squeers and Nicholas share gender ('he'-class).

clauses: "Some things," replied his mother, "you can never play cricket, as every Crofton boy would like to do; you can never dance at your sister's Christmas parties."
"O mamma!" cried Agnes, with tears in her eyes, thinking it cruel to talk so.
"Go on!" cried Hugh, brightening. "You know what I feel, mother, and even sister Agnes sometimes makes out that it is no misfortune."
"There will be little checks and mortifications continually, when you see little boys leaping over this, while you must stand out," said the mother.
"O mamma!" exclaimed Agnes.
"Well, and what else?" said Hugh.
note: Hugh (disabled boy), his sister Agnes, and their mother discussing Hugh's condition; Agnes and mother share gender ('she'-class) while Hugh is re-named every turn (no ambiguity for him) -- a PARTIAL same-gender-ambiguity case, useful contrast to fully-ambiguous scenes, isolating whether a discriminator over-triggers ambiguity handling when only a subset of entities actually share gender.

clauses: "Have confidence in me a few moments," said Omar; "accept Ali's bargain; let me choose in your stead."
"Here it is," said Ali; "it weighs twenty pounds. Choose what you will."
The stranger, beside himself with joy, took three diamonds and forced them on Omar, who put them in his girdle, and seated himself by his father.
"Well done," said Mansour; "but it is my turn now; mark me well, and profit by the lesson I shall give you."
"What I desire," said Mansour, "is the casket with all its contents; this young man has promised to give me what I please."
"It is mere child's play," answered Omar; "but since you desire it, my father, you shall lose your suit."
"Illustrious cadi," said Omar, "this young man is ready to fulfill his engagement; this is what he offers Mansour."
"No one," interrupted the cadi, "and I least of all; the necklace is worth a hundred thousand piasters, is it not, Mansour?"
note: Five male entities (Omar, Ali, Mansour, the Banian/stranger, the cadi) in a courtroom bargaining scene with continuous same-gender pronoun chains; clause 2 'seated himself by his father' requires resolving 'his father'=Mansour, introduced only by RELATION (not proper name) in the same clause as Omar -- one of the hardest coref configurations mined, a possessive-relation antecedent not yet lexically named at point of first use.

clauses: A certain man saw it, and told Joab, and said, Behold, I saw Absalom hanged in an oak.
Joab said unto the man, Why didst thou not smite him there to the ground?
The man said unto Joab, I would not put forth my hand against the king's son.
Then said Joab, I may not tarry thus with thee; and he took three darts, and thrust them through the heart of Absalom.
Then said Ahimaaz, the son of Zadok, Let me now run, and bear the king tidings.
And Joab said unto him, Thou shalt not bear tidings this day; then said Joab to Cushi, Go, tell the king what thou hast seen.
And Ahimaaz said again to Joab, let me also run after Cushi; and Joab said, Wherefore wilt thou run, my son?
Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and overran Cushi.
note: Five-plus male named entities (Joab, an unnamed man, Absalom, Ahimaaz, Cushi, plus King David referenced) in a dense biblical reported-speech chain; every clause is 'X said (unto) Y' with all-male referents. Clause 1 'Joab said unto the man, Why didst thou not smite HIM' -- 'him' = Absalom, a THIRD entity that is neither speaker nor addressee, the sharpest same-gender trap in the set (pronoun refers outside the current speech-act dyad).
